extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics educators, and researchers in undergraduate mathematics education
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for modifying mathematical proofs to improve their pedagogical quality for second- and third-year undergraduate students, based on mathematicians' judgments. Includes specific modification types tested and the measurement/scoring approach used to evaluate changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit hypothesis and conclusion statements (make proof framework explicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof for undergraduates can be improved if a hypothesis and conclusion statements are added to the proof that make explicit the proof framework being employed (Selden & Selden, 1995). In many undergraduate proofs, these are not explicitly stated and the proof framework is implicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add explicit 'To show...' or 'Therefore...' sentences so the overall structure and target of the argument is clear to students (example: M1 modification added explicit injectivity goal and concluding sentence). Expected to improve understandability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize important equations via typesetting/formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasizing important equations in a proof via typesetting (e.g., centering important formulas on their own lines) will improve the quality of the proof because it makes clear the proof's main ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format key equations so they stand out (example: M2 reformatted two formulas as centered lines). Such formatting helps students identify and follow central steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add extra justification for assertions that students might not infer
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding extra justification to support an assertion can improve the clarity of a proof if that justification might be difficult for a student to infer on their own (tested as M3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide additional justification selectively where typical students are unlikely to make the inference themselves. Note: the study found no consensus—some mathematicians thought extra justification helps, others that it removes productive cognitive struggle or was poorly worded—so exercise judgment about level and wording of added justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary or irrelevant computations/assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Including unnecessary irrelevant computations or assumptions in a proof will make the proof worse since this will unnecessarily lengthen the proof and confuse students (hypothesis H4; examples M4 and M5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insert correct but unhelpful algebraic manipulations or irrelevant assumptions (e.g., 'so x2-x1 = ...' when it adds no insight, or restating irrelevant domain assumptions). Such insertions were judged by participants to reduce pedagogical quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity as a pedagogical virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of pedagogy, brevity is a desirable attribute of a proof: shorter, more concise proofs are preferred so long as essential structure and clarity are preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concise exposition; remove superfluous steps, but balance brevity against the need to make framework and essential justifications explicit for learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate level of justification (balance between explicitness and student inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriate amount of justification in a pedagogical proof must balance clarity for students with encouraging their inferential development; mathematicians do not agree on a single correct level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide on justification depth based on target students' abilities and instructional goals. The study's mixed responses to M3 show some participants prefer pushing students to infer some steps, while others prefer more explicit support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie formal proofs to informal arguments and overarching structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should be more closely tied to informal arguments, make explicit the proof’s overarching structure while suppressing unnecessary logical detail, or be illustrated with carefully chosen generic examples (recommendations from literature: Hersh, Leron, Rowland, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use informal motivation and structural signposting to show 'why' a result holds, not only 'that' it holds. Use a generic illustrative example where appropriate to demonstrate methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation/Scoring scale for judging modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants judged whether changes to a proof made it 'significantly better', 'somewhat better', 'the proofs were the same', 'somewhat worse', or 'significantly worse', which the authors coded as 2, 1, 0, -1, -2 respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This five-point Likert-like scale was used in a repeated-measures design with randomized presentation order; statistical comparisons (means, ANOVA) determine whether a modification significantly differs from zero (no change). Example results: M1 mean 1.29*, M2 mean 1.05*, M3 mean 0.02, M4 mean -1.66*, M5 mean -1.12* (asterisk indicates mean significantly different from zero with p<0.001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of concrete modification exemplars when evaluating proof quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations of 'better' or 'worse' were made by showing participants a master proof and a modified proof with changes highlighted (blue) so evaluators could directly compare specific alterations (M1–M5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or revising pedagogical proofs, present concrete before/after examples and solicit specific commentary; the option for free-text explanation revealed reasons behind judgments (e.g., clarity vs. pedagogical challenge).
